# Reflection — RORORO v1.18.0 "Settings becomes a place"

> **Note:** This feedback is AI-generated. It's observational, not authoritative. Use what's useful.

Cart cycle #6 on this repo. Thirteen findings-register rows, one surface, fourteen items against
twelve planned, fifteen commits, two checkpoints. Suite 1427 → 1490 with no regression at any step.
Merged as PR #107; the F-091 correction followed as PR #108.

---

## Scope & Idea Clarity

**What landed:** The cluster was picked from data rather than instinct. All 51 open rows were bucketed
by fix affinity before anything was written — Preferences 13, accessible naming 9, copy 8, dialog
vocabulary 5, button/banner 3, tail 13 — and Settings won on coherence per row, not on count. The
sharper move is the section titled *"The two rows that are not really Preferences, named rather than
smuggled."* F-037 is a nine-window sweep and F-046 reaches into F-068's 61-site territory. Both were
kept, both were labelled as edges, and `/spec` was handed an explicit instruction about where F-046's
line had to hold. Quietly counting them as Preferences rows is exactly how a 13-row cycle becomes a
61-site one.

**What to tighten:** The scope promised a number: *"Register goes from 51 open to 38."* It sits at
**41**. The arithmetic is exact and worth reading — 51 minus the 12 rows that closed is 39, plus
F-093 and F-094, which this cycle opened. Nothing went wrong; a remediation cycle that reads code
carefully **generates** findings, and that is the cycle working. But a net-register target treats the
register as a burn-down when it is a discovery log, and it makes a successful cycle look like it
missed. State the target as rows closed, and predict the opens as a range instead of pretending
they're zero.

## Requirements Thinking

**What landed:** One acceptance criterion in Story 1.1 that no register row asked for: a value outside
a sensible range must be refused visibly, because *"a megabyte field that accepts `-1` silently is the
same defect one level down."* Every row in this cluster is a variant of "the app knows something and
does not say it," and generalizing the pattern rather than transcribing the list is what a PRD is
supposed to do. The same instinct produced the cycle's one durable new mechanism — a settings-schema
test that fails the build when a persisted field has no UI. F-023 survived months because nothing
connected *persisted* to *reachable*; the row was a symptom of a missing check, and the PRD said so.

**What to tighten:** The PRD's own header states that every claim about current behaviour was
re-verified against the tree. That held for the rows and did not hold for the prose written around
them. It said one setting spoke in first person — three did. It prescribed *"reopen this page"* as the
fix for a tooltip promising an unnecessary restart, but the rail's five pages are one window with
toggled `Visibility`, so reopening re-lists nothing. That one traded a false promise for a different
false promise and survived to item 7. The re-verification discipline is real; extend it to anything
the PRD newly asserts, not only to the rows it inherits.

## Technical Decisions

**What landed:** The highest-rated row in the cluster dissolved on inspection. F-026 (`4/5`) asks for
"a level above the card." `SectionHeadingStyle` ships at
[`ControlStyles.xaml:143`](../src/ROROROblox.App/Controls/ControlStyles.xaml#L143) as
`13px / SemiBold / WhiteBrush / Margin 0,18,0,6` — not merely available, but *the same thing the page
was already writing by hand*, with an 18-above/6-below margin that is precisely the missing level. The
answer was to place it **between** cards instead of inside one. No new primitive, which is what the
PRD required, because a second container primitive is the two-meanings defect restated.

Second: item 2 was placed **before** item 3 so the reachability fence would go red naming the four
unreachable watchdog settings, and item 3 would turn it green. A fence written after its fix proves
nothing. That ordering was chosen deliberately and the checklist cites why.

**What to tighten:** `AppSettings.cs` was cited as living in `App` in the spec, the PRD **and** the
checklist — with the line numbers correct. That is the citation shape that survives review, because
the part a reader spot-checks is the part that's right. It lives in `Core`. Running `git ls-files`
against every path a planning doc cites costs about a minute and would have caught it in all three
documents at once.

## Plan vs. Reality

**What landed:** Fourteen items against twelve, and both additions were earned rather than drift. 4a
came out of C1 and the fence hardening came out of the fence failing its own proof. Then the harder
one: **F-046 was not flipped.** Item 10's abort condition never fired — every site resolved by lookup
rather than by taste — but holding that line left `PluginsWindow`'s Remove a hand-rolled magenta fill,
which is verbatim the row's headline evidence. Twelve of thirteen is the honest number, and reporting
twelve when the process would have tolerated thirteen is the part worth keeping.

**What to tighten:** The suite constructs no `Window`, by design, so every on-screen claim is owed to a
human. This session produced two real defects that 1490 passing tests could not see — a 6px selection
dot rendering off-centre, and a plugin that had stopped following the host theme. Both were caught by
looking at the running app. The rendered gate v1.17 added is the right seam to grow: it samples pixels
today but asserts nothing about layout. Geometry assertions on the controls that already have a
rendering harness would move a class of defect out of the human's column.

## How You Worked

**What landed:** The C1 intervention, in one sentence: *"I think we need some default set based on the
user system in the memory section. If we don't want to pull the system, then we can ask the user to
enter their memory size. Go on everything else."* That became item 4a, and the catch was about the
**pattern**, not the control — blank-means-automatic without saying what automatic resolves to is this
cycle's own defect one level down, on a page built to fix that defect. The app already knew:
`ISystemMemoryProbe` was in DI and `MemoryDefaults` derived both values at startup. Surfacing it was
the work; deriving it was not. Separately, the cycle's three hard exclusions (F-050, F-091, F-068)
were set unprompted before scope opened, and all three held to the end.

**What to tighten:** Two checkpoints in a fourteen-item cycle, and both of them found something — C1
produced 4a, and the C2 walk caught a rejected test theme whose root cause turned out to be a doc
comment that had been lying since v1.11. That is a 100% hit rate on eyes-on gates, which argues for
more of them, not the same number. Place checkpoints by **evidence type** rather than by item count:
the items whose proof is on screen (hierarchy across four themes, the destructive-button rank under
flatline, compact mode across a real restart) are the ones the suite structurally cannot cover, and
they're the ones that should gate.

## Your Goals

The stated target was *"close the 13-row Preferences/Settings cluster, register 51 open → 38"* against
a quality bar of consistency — *"a page named for a feature that is not on it fails the same test a
broken tile does."*

Twelve of thirteen rows closed. Alerts & memory holds memory controls. A failed theme write says so
instead of reverting silently at restart. Compact mode survives a restart. Sections read as sections
without a second card. Six settings in three voices became nine settings in one, in second person.
The bar was met on the surface it was aimed at.

The one thing that would take it further is the thing the numbers already hint at: **F-046 stayed open
because the vocabulary it depends on lives in F-068's 61 un-migrated sites.** Three cycles have now
routed around that migration. It is the largest single consistency debt in the app, it is flat at 61
across five days, and every cycle that avoids it inherits an exception. It is the next cycle that buys
the most.

## Reflection

The dominant pattern in this cycle was not a bug class. It was **five separate instances of a check
reporting success while measuring something other than what it claims**, all in the same session:

1. Checklist `--filter "Foo*|Bar*"` fields matching **zero tests** — VSTest's grammar has no glob
   wildcards, and the run reports success having executed nothing. That shipped in every Verify field
   of the v1.17 checklist; a checkpoint could have been signed off on nothing having run.
2. A pre-commit hook scanning only staged files while its CI twin sat red for seven hours.
3. A rendered contrast gate whose sampling model could not fail the proof its own design nominated.
4. A centring test that passed against markup deliberately broken three different ways — deleted
   rather than shipped.
5. The reachability fence reading a doc comment as evidence of reachability, so a setting could stay
   green forever on the strength of a comment *about* it.

**Every one of them looked exactly like coverage.** The cycle's other headline number belongs to the
same family: fourteen false claims found, and most of them were in our own artifacts rather than the
code. A path wrong with the line numbers right. Two stale counts inside a fence's own failure
messages. A doc comment that said camelCase when the format is snake_case, which silently vanishes any
theme written to its instructions — F-053's exact complaint, *caused by* the documentation meant to
prevent it.

The operating lesson is narrow and worth keeping: **a green check is a claim, and claims from your own
tooling get verified the same way claims from the register do — against the tree.** The register
already codifies this ("verify against the tree, never a changelog"). This cycle showed the rule
applies one level up, to the gates themselves.
